papers.title: Dynamic allocation of MurJ coordinates bacterial growth and division
papers.abstract: Rod-shaped bacteria grow by inserting peptidoglycan into the lateral cell wall during elongation and into the septal cell wall during division. These two modes of growth are driven by distinct peptidoglycan synthesis machineries that consume the shared precursor Lipid II and must be coordinated so that cell enlargement remains matched to division. However, how cells spatially allocate this shared precursor, and whether Lipid II translocation itself contributes to this coordi-nation, remain unclear. Here we show that the spatial distribution of the essential Lipid II flippase MurJ coordinates this balance in Escherichia coli. Increasing nonseptal MurJ abundance shifted cell-wall synthesis toward elongation and reduced septal synthesis. Single-molecule tracking revealed that MurJ diffuses throughout the membrane but is transiently captured at the division site, rather than stably incorporated into the septal synthesis machinery. This recruitment requires active septal cell-wall synthesis, but not ongoing Lipid II synthesis or flipping, indicating that MurJ recruitment is coupled to the active synthesis machinery rather than to substrate availability or transport. Thus, activation of septal synthesis creates transient MurJ capture at the division site, providing a mechanism to preferentially supply Lipid II for septal growth during cytokinesis. These findings reveal a capture-and-release mechanism that dynamically enriches MurJ at active division sites and thereby coordinates elongation and division in bacterial cells.

papers.title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates
papers.abstract: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous {beta}-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.

papers.title: A Urinary Metabolomic Signature Associated with Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Children with Short Bowel Syndrome
papers.abstract: Direct sampling of the small intestinal microbiome is challenging. Urinary metabolites may offer a noninvasive approach to studying microbial functional activity. We used clinically available gas chromatography/mass spectrometry to profile urinary organic acids in 94 children with short bowel syndrome, comparing those with clinically defined small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO; n=21) with those without SIBO (n=73). SIBO-associated metabolites included microbial fermentation products, dietary derivatives, and host metabolic intermediates. Metabolites enriched in SIBO mapped to aromatic amino acid metabolism, including tryptophan and tyrosine pathways, consistent with altered microbial fermentation. Many associations persisted after adjustment for intestinal anatomy, age, antibiotic exposure, and nutritional composition. These findings identified a urinary metabolic profile associated with clinically defined SIBO in children with short bowel syndrome and support further evaluation of urinary metabolomics as a noninvasive approach to studying small intestinal microbial function.

papers.title: Second-site capsule-locus mutations, not Ade efflux disruption, determine phage susceptibility across an Acinetobacter baumannii transposon mutant panel
papers.abstract: Resistance-Nodulation-Division (RND) efflux pumps have been implicated in phage adsorption in several Gram-negative bacteria, suggesting that AdeABC, AdeFGH and AdeIJK, the three characterised RND efflux systems of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, could play a similar role. We tested this hypothesis using five phages (Equilibrator, Taro, AT01, BB02, and AC03) and a panel of 13 A. baumannii strains, including nine AB5075 transposon mutants affecting AdeABC, AdeFGH, or AdeIJK. Host-range testing, efficiency-of-plating assays, capsule-associated density measurements, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing were performed to assess the relationship between genotype and phage infection. Overall, the data did not support a role for the Ade components as receptors. Phages Equilibrator, Taro and AT01 formed plaques on every strain, and the restricted host ranges of BB02 and AC03 did not correspond to disruption of a particular efflux system. Sequencing instead identified second-site mutations in the KL25 capsule locus in six of the ten AB5075 strains. These included a 1,998-bp deletion affecting wzc, substitutions in mnaA and mnaB, an ISAba13 insertion in a putative glycosyltransferase and a subpopulation-associated frameshift in wzx. AC03 formed plaques on all six strains with capsule-locus changes but on none of the five strains without them. Capsule dependence differed among the other phages: relative to the parental AB5075, infection by these phages, Equilibrator, Taro and BB02, was restricted on the capsule-deficient wzc::T26 strain, whereas AT01 efficiency was only slightly reduced. Insertion-site mapping also distinguished a near-terminal adeK insertion that retained the parental antimicrobial phenotype from an early adeK insertion associated with loss of AdeIJK function. Together, these findings identify capsule-locus variation as the strongest correlation with phage susceptibility in this panel and demonstrate the importance of verifying mutant genomes before assigning phenotypes to their annotated insertions.

papers.title: A Staphylococcus phage recombination cassette that enables recombineering across distant bacteria
papers.abstract: Modifying bacterial genomes with phage recombinases, a process termed recombineering, has enabled precise genome editing, but its reach is limited by host specificity: each new organism generally requires its own recombinase to be identified and optimized. Using known phage recombination genes as synteny anchors, we mined Staphylococcus genomes and recovered a diverse collection of phage recombination cassettes, spanning the RAD52-like annealase superfamily (Sak, Erf) and the RAD51/RecA-like Sak4 family. Functional testing of representatives in S. aureus identified several highly efficient systems that support recombineering. We engineered the most efficient of these into a single-plasmid tool that yields markerless editing in S. aureus in four days. Notably, where other recombineering systems rely on host-specific factors for nuclease evasion and ssDNA loading, this cassette encodes both activities itself: a predicted broad-spectrum nuclease inhibitor and a dedicated single-stranded DNA-binding protein. We therefore tested the cassette across phylogenetically distant hosts, and observed recombination in Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecium, Francisella novicida, and Escherichia coli. These results identify a self-sufficient class of phage recombination systems and provide a portable tool for

papers.title: Higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals gate pathobiont expansion through succinate-driven pH modulation
papers.abstract: Despite advances in defining microbiome shifts associated with inflammatory mucosal diseases, the ecological interactions that constrain or facilitate pathobiont expansion remain poorly understood. Using a six-species synthetic oral microbial community and factorial interaction screening, we identified a higher-order interaction governing the growth of the periodontal pathobiont Porphyromonas gingivalis. The core community member Veillonella parvula was the strongest positive determinant of P. gingivalis growth, but this effect was substantially reduced by the health-associated commensal Actinomyces oris. A. oris-mediated antagonism resulted from extracellular acidification and was enhanced under anaerobic conditions. Genetic dissection of A. oris fermentation revealed that lactate dehydrogenase (ldh1) contributes to anaerobic lactate production, but ldh1 deletion only partially relieved P. gingivalis inhibition. Instead, succinate, produced through a succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase pathway (sdh2), emerged as the principal driver of acidification and P. gingivalis suppression. At high cell densities, however, V. parvula consumed both lactate and succinate, reversing acidification and restoring conditions permissive for P. gingivalis growth. To assess the relevance of these interactions in vivo, we analyzed subgingival microbiome from 1,355 adults, including 555 with detectable P. gingivalis. Among these individuals, P. gingivalis abundance was negatively associated with Actinomyces abundance after adjustment for periodontitis severity, whereas this association was attenuated at high V. parvula abundance, consistent with the interaction observed in vitro. Together, these findings identify succinate as a previously unrecognized mediator of interbacterial antagonism and reveal how higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals regulate pathobiont expansion through pH modulation, with protective effects shaped by oxygen availability and metabolic cross-feeding.

papers.title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
papers.abstract: Background Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus) system comprising free-living mice (Wild:As), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like:As), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like:As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory Mus musculus (Lab-like:As). We compared these three Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory Mus musculus (Lab:Mm) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions. Results We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab:Mm and Lab-like:As than in Wild:As and Wild-like:As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild:As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like:As mice remained most similar to Wild:As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like:As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like:As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab:Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in [≥]90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild:As to 46 in Wild-like:As, 72 in Lab-like:As, and 138 in Lab:Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild:As and Wild-like:As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like:As shifted toward the Lab:Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct. Conclusions Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.

papers.title: Bayesian phylogenetic inference accounting for recombination in whole bacterial genomes
papers.abstract: Recombination is a major evolutionary force in bacteria, and ignoring it distorts phylogenies and can invalidate downstream analyses such as dating. We present ClonalFrame2, a new software for Bayesian phylogenetic inference from whole bacterial genomes that accounts for recombination. It replaces both ClonalFrame and ClonalFrameML while using the same evolutionary model, in which both mutation and recombination events occur on the branches of the clonal genealogy. The locations of recombination events are integrated out of the likelihood using a hidden Markov model, so the algorithm targets only the clonal genealogy and three recombination parameters. Ancestral sequences are recomputed whenever the tree changes and are used to propose efficient topology updates. We validated the method by analysing data-free datasets, which recovered the prior, and by comparing the approximated likelihood with the exact one on simulated data. Across 100 simulated datasets of 100 genomes each, the recombination parameters were accurately recovered, and trees inferred while accounting for recombination were many times more accurate than when ignoring it. In Staphylococcus aureus ST239, we showed that accounting for recombination gave a stronger temporal signal and a more robust dated phylogeny. In Neisseria gonorrhoeae, we identified interesting patterns of clustered recombination events happening repeatedly across the branches of the tree.

papers.title: Orsay virus infection is associated with reduced locomotion and alters cue-dependent food choice in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Behavioral responses are an important component of host defense; however, most evidence in Caenorhabditis elegans comes from bacterial pathogens. Here, we tested whether infection with Orsay virus (OrV) alters host dispersal and food choice and whether these responses involve the RNA-processing factor EOL-1. When measuring distance travelled over a certain period of time in control and infected wild-type animals, we observed that OrV infection was associated with lower locomotion. Moreover, when presenting infected and control animals with food choices, we observed that infected animals preferred OrV infected food sources only when the alternative was a pure food source, preferring a non-inoculated food source when both control and viral food sources contained a C. elegans filtrate. Moreover, loss of EOL-1 altered baseline locomotion and attenuated the infection-associated reduction detected in the earlier motility assay, while also modifying the food choice response, suggesting that eol-1 contributes to the motility and behavioral changes induced by OrV infection. Collectively, these results support an overall association between OrV infection and reduced host dispersal, whereas its effect on food choice depends on the sensory context. These findings extend infection-associated behavioral responses to a natural viral pathogen and identify eol-1 as a modulator of their expression.

papers.title: Phenotypic and Molecular Characterization of Potentially New Shigella boydii Serotype in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Objective: Shigella is a major cause of bacillary dysentery among children under 5 years of age, especially in low- and middle-income countries. At Dhaka hospital of icddr,b, every year around 3% of Shigella isolates from patients with diarrhea are identified as Shigella-like organisms (SLOs). These isolates do not react with any of the existing and provisional Shigella antisera. The major aims of the present study were to characterize a unique cluster of SLOs using phenotypic and genotypic methods. Methods: A cluster of 6 SLOs was characterized using biochemical tests, serotyping, antimicrobial susceptibility, and virulence assay by using the Sereny test, PCR and compared their pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) patterns with known serotypes of Shigella spp. Antisera against the isolate were raised in a rabbit model to determine cross-reactivity with known serotypes. Results: All six SLOs were mannitol fermenting, have invasive properties, positive for ipaH and Shigella enterotoxin 2 gene along with possession of virulence plasmid of ~ 140 MDa. All isolates were resistant to ampicillin, tetracycline, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, but were sensitive to mecillinam, nalidixic acid, and ciprofloxacin. Plasmid and PFGE profiles showed that the genomic patterns of these isolates were identical but were different from all other S. boydii serotypes. Antiserum prepared against one of the isolates agglutinated with all isolates but did not cross-react with other Shigella and E. coli reference strains. Conclusion: This unique cluster of isolates might belong to a new provisional serovar of S. boydii and further analysis is required to incorporate it into the stereotypic scheme of Shigella.

papers.title: The Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretome exerts antimicrobial activity against Burkholderia glumae by disrupting cell envelope homeostasis and impairing bacterial replication
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of antimicrobials used to manage bacterial infections is increasingly threatened by the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Many conventional antimicrobials act on a single defined target that pathogens can circumvent through target modification or pathway adaptation. In contrast, antimicrobials that disrupt multiple cellular processes may impose greater fitness costs and reduce the likelihood of resistance development, making their discovery a priority for pharmaceutical and agricultural applications. We previously demonstrated that the environmental bacterium Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretes a complex mixture of molecules (secretome) with antimicrobial activity against several plants and human pathogens. However, the mechanism underlying this activity remained unknown. Here, we used the plant pathogen Burkholderia glumae to investigate the mode of action of the P. protegens PBL3 secretome. We showed that the P. protegens PLB3 secretome causes extensive cell envelope damage that results in cell death and interferes with bacterial multiplication. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed broad disruption of processes associated with cell-envelope biogenesis and homeostasis and bacterial replication. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the P. protegens PBL3 secretome acts as a multi-target antimicrobial that could be harnessed in the development of therapeutics to control bacterial infections of agricultural and medical importance.

papers.title: Long-read shotgun metagenomics identifies distinct urogenital microbial community states associated with functional potential and urinary tract infection during pregnancy
papers.abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections during pregnancy and are associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Although previous studies used enhanced culture, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and/or short-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize the urogenital microbiome of adult females, few have assessed the urogenital microbiome during pregnancy and thus this microbiome remains poorly understood. Here, we applied Oxford Nanopore long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize urogenital microbial composition, functional potential, metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), and the urogenital virome of pregnant females. Taxonomic profiling identified three distinct microbial community states predominated by Lactobacillus crispatus, Gardnerella species, and L. iners. The Gardnerella-predominated community was associated with a higher frequency of UTI during pregnancy. Functional profiles strongly reflected these community states, demonstrating that taxonomic differences were accompanied by distinct functional potential. Genome-resolved analysis recovered 415 MAGs, including 29 high-quality genomes, revealing substantial genomic diversity among urogenital microbes. Viral sequences, predominantly bacteriophages, also were detected in most samples, highlighting an additional component of the pregnancy-associated urogenital microbiome. These findings demonstrate that pregnant females possess distinct urogenital microbial community states and show that they differ not only in taxonomic composition but also in their functional potential.

papers.title: Gut Roseburia hominis-derived 10-hydroxystearic acid alleviates metabolic disorder by restoring hepatic fatty acid metabolism
papers.abstract: Metabolic disorders and health-promoting dietary interventions represent complementary contexts of metabolic impairment and improvement, providing an opportunity to identify gut microbial taxa associated with both disease status and dietary response. Here, we integrated five independent human cohorts spanning metabolic disorders and dietary interventions and identified Roseburia hominis as a gut microbial taxon that consistently decreased in metabolic disorders and increased after dietary interventions. Beyond species abundance, strain-level genetic variation in R. hominis provided additional information for distinguishing metabolic disorder status and stratifying cardiometabolic severity. Integration of phenotype-associated variants with circulating metabolomics prioritized ohyA, encoding an oleate hydratase, as a candidate functional determinant linking R. hominis genetic variation to host metabolic heterogeneity. An ohyA-based genetic burden score was associated with adverse cardiometabolic traits and changed longitudinally during dietary intervention, while circulating metabolites statistically accounted for part of the associations between ohyA variants and host phenotypes. Functional experiments demonstrated that R. hominis OhyA protein converts oleic acid to 10-hydroxystearic acid (10-HSA), whereas an OhyA carrying five prioritized missense substitutions showed markedly impaired enzymatic activity. In high-fat diet-fed mice, 10-HSA attenuated body-weight gain, improved glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, and reduced dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. Multi-omics profiling revealed limited remodeling of the gut microbiota but pronounced hepatic transcriptional and metabolic responses, characterized by activation of PPAR-associated lipid-metabolic pathways, altered fatty-acid oxidation and desaturation, and remodeling of hepatic lipid composition. Together, these findings establish a diet-responsive R. hominis-OhyA-10-HSA axis linking microbial variation to host metabolic dysfunction and show that 10-HSA can improve metabolic health in mice.

papers.title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity
papers.abstract: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina. Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2{Delta} complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, {beta}-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced {beta}-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2{Delta} mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1, RLM1, FKS2/GSC2, GFA1, CHS1, CRH1, SED1, and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1, GAS1, GAS3, and CHS2 expression. Expression of either Pjpgm2 or Pmpgm2 broadly shifted these responses toward wild-type levels. Selected transcriptional changes were further evaluated by qRT-PCR, which supported the major stress and cell-wall responses identified by RNA sequencing. FKS2/GSC2 showed the same directional pattern, although differences were not statistically significant by qRT-PCR. Despite this compensatory response, Pgm2-deficient cells were markedly more susceptible to sublethal caspofungin, whereas either Pneumocystis Pgm2 homolog restored tolerance toward wild-type levels. These findings link Pgm2-dependent glucose-phosphate metabolism with {beta}-1,3-glucan levels and cell-wall function. Given the importance of {beta}-1,3-glucan to the Pneumocystis cyst wall and its limited cell-wall biosynthetic pathways, these findings further support Pgm2 as an important component of Pneumocystis cell-wall biology and a potential antifungal target.

papers.title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting
papers.abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase in vitro, type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets in vivo, suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference. These findings identify RNA polymerase backtracking as a key determinant of Cas10-Csm activity and support a model in which arrested transcription complexes generate substrates for DNA degradation, opening up new anti-CRISPR strategies against type III.

papers.title: Temperature alters Culex tarsalis West Nile virus vector competence, tissue bottlenecks, and transcriptional responses
papers.abstract: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Temperature is frequently the strongest abiotic factor impacting transmission in many virus-vector pairings, including WNV and Culex. However, it is unknown how temperature impacts WNV population bottlenecks and transcriptional responses to infection in Culex tarsalis. We found that elevated temperatures led to increased likelihood of transmission of rare virus variants due to increased vector competence and less stringent tissue barriers. Analysis of Cx. tarsalis transcriptional responses confirmed that WNV infection had minimal impacts on transcriptional activity. Temperature, however, induced significant changes to mosquito gene expression, whereas canonical immune gene expression minimally changed in response to infection. Thus, temperature impacts bottlenecks in the Culex-WNV system independent of known antiviral pathways, possibly by altering virus replication dynamics. While temperature had a dramatic impact on bottleneck stringency, this is likely independent of antiviral pathways and instead some other change to mosquito biology. Together, these results shed light on the relationships between temperature, virus evolutionary dynamics and antiviral immunity.

papers.title: Replication-coupled maturation of readthrough late transcripts by a polyomavirus small T antigen
papers.abstract: Productive polyomavirus gene expression requires the maturation of long, non-polyadenylated "wraparound" transcripts generated by late-strand readthrough of the polyadenylation signal on the circular genome, giving rise to structural protein mRNAs and microRNAs. In Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV), small T (sT) antigen, along with large T (LT) antigen-mediated DNA replication, drives this process. Deletion of sT (MCV{Delta}sT) attenuates late gene transcription, abolishes splicing, eliminates VP1 expression, and traps unspliced transcripts in the nucleus. Exogenous sT restored transcription and splicing in an aphidicolin-sensitive manner, requiring domains that activate DNA replication and bind chromatin. RNA sequencing revealed that sT promotes splicing and polyadenylation of wraparound transcripts, thereby increasing cytoplasmic VP1 and VP2 mRNA levels. A dual-fluorescence reporter confirmed that the leaky late poly(A) signal (LpA) was used more efficiently upon sT expression, indicating enhanced polyadenylation. Co-expression with LT abolished this effect, likely by overwhelming the capacity of the polyadenylation machinery. sT from HPyV7 and HPyV9 could similarly rescue this defect, indicating that this regulatory activity is conserved in a subset of sT proteins. Together, these findings define sT as a replication-coupled regulator of late transcript expression, splicing, and polyadenylation, revealing how a compact DNA virus converts readthrough transcription into productive gene expression.

papers.title: RubisCO-encoding methanotrophs elicit a coordinated transcriptional response to carbon dioxide limitation.
papers.abstract: The methanotroph Methylococcus capsulatus encodes the carbon dioxide (CO2)-fixing enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RubisCO), which, along with CO2 and methane (CH4), are required for growth of this bacterium. This unique, dual one-carbon metabolism is present in phylogenetically diverse methanotrophs and is likely widespread in nature, but the connection between organic and inorganic carbon metabolism in these methanotrophs is unclear. Here we used a systems approach to investigate the requisite role of CO2 in M. capsulatus metabolism and physiology. We show that atmospheric CO2 levels are sufficient for M. capsulatus cultivation, and that CO2 assimilation is linked to cellular redox balance. In the absence of CO2, M. capsulatus elicits a global transcriptional response that includes induction of RubisCO- and other inorganic carbon assimilation-encoding genes with a concomitant decrease in ribosome biogenesis and nitrogen assimilation genes typical of a bacterial stringent response. This CO2 starvation response balances biosynthesis with carbon availability. Genetic and biochemical evidence show that a LysR-type transcriptional regulator (CbbR) activates RubisCO and other CO2 assimilation gene transcription via direct promoter binding in response to elevated intracellular RubisCO substrate, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, in CO2-starved cells. These results offer insights into the essentiality of CO2 for M. capsulatus metabolism and establish a function for CbbR-family regulators in methanotrophs beyond their canonical association with CO2 fixation in autotrophic bacteria.

papers.title: Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs) spreading antimicrobial resistance, host-adaptation factors and defense systems, a novel satellite family of nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae
papers.abstract: Phage satellites are mobile genetic elements that depend on helper bacteriophages to promote their own dissemination. Here, we identified a novel family of large satellites, named Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs), that are widespread in Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica among diverse hosts, worldwide. These largest satellites to date (71.6 {+/-} 15.8 kbp) are specifically transduced by the persistent jumbo bacteriophage Goslarvirus of the nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae family. Furthermore, PICJIs carried numerous accessory genes associated with clinically relevant antimicrobial resistances, host-adaptation, and several anti-phage defense systems.

papers.title: Functional genomic characterization of anti-phage defense systems in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium
papers.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a significant public health threat, demonstrating high rates of antibiotic resistance and frequently causing hospital-acquired infections. Bacteriophages (phages) are a promising adjunctive therapy to reduce bacterial load and manage VREfm infections. Many bacteria encode anti-phage defense systems--groups of genes that can counteract phage infection--but these systems have not been characterized in VREfm. Here we explored the diversity of anti-phage defense systems within clinical VREfm isolate genomes and examined their impact on phage susceptibility. We first used two available bioinformatic tools (DefenseFinder and PADLOC) to identify putative anti-phage defense systems in 21 hybrid-assembled VREfm clinical isolate genomes, and observed that most anti-phage defense systems were located on plasmids, defense islands, and prophages. Combining this information with functional testing of phage susceptibility did not reveal robust associations between specific defense systems and resistance to four VREfm-targeting lytic phages. Due to inherent limitations of phage susceptibility testing, we next developed an assay to assess phage survival after co-incubation with bacteria, and identified over two dozen genes associated with phage killing, including a potentially novel defense island. Lastly, we attempted to functionally validate 10 candidate anti-phage defense systems, only four of which were ultimately tested in enterococci. Expression of one of these candidates, AbiE, decreased bacterial susceptibility to two Enterococcus-targeting phages. As VREfm-targeting phage therapy becomes more widely available, identification of genes contributing to phage resistance can aid in streamlining the provision of phages to patients who could benefit from this new therapeutic modality.

papers.title: The YjfJ protein is the effector of a second PspA/VIPP1 system that is widespread in the Gammaproteobacteria
papers.abstract: Maintaining the integrity of the cytoplasmic membrane is essential for bacterial cell survival. Unsurprisingly, prokaryotes have evolved conserved mechanisms by which they sense, maintain, and repair membrane integrity in response to stress. The phage shock protein (Psp) is one such system, understood primarily through work undertaken in the Gammaproteobacterial species Escherichia coli and Yersinia enterocolitica. The system utilises an effector, PspA, alongside accessory proteins that sense stress and recruit PspA to damaged membranes. Homologues of PspA - part of the PspA/VIPP1 family - are found in a variety of bacterial phyla. Although most work in the Gammaproteobacteria has concerned the canonical Psp response, there have been descriptions of non-canonical PspA/VIPP1-containing systems that warrant further genomic analysis. By analysing the PspA/VIPP1 content of a diverse selection of Gammaproteobacterial genomes, we reveal the existence of two phylogenetically distinct subtypes of PspA/VIPP1 proteins, PspA- and YjfJ-like, which are found at similar frequencies. The YjfJ-like proteins are not only a novel subtype of PspA/VIPP1, having their own unique set of accessory proteins, but in some species, such as the ESKAPE pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, comprise the only PspA/VIPP1-containing system. Our study positions the YjfJ-like containing systems on equal footing with the PspA system in terms of their conservation and distribution in the Gammaproteobacteria. This suggests that studies into the biological functions of YjfJ-like proteins would be well-justified from their unique presence in some important human pathogens.

papers.title: Lung Epithelial TLR7 is a Factor in Viral Replication and Pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Respiratory virus infections are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality of infants and the elderly worldwide. Currently it is not known how Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccination of infants can cause enhancement of RSV disease, highlighting gaps in our understanding about how viruses like RSV interact with the immune system. Here we address this and show that ERK MAP kinase signaling from Toll-like Receptor-7 (TLR7) detection of RSV and influenza, but not human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3), infections in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) drives replication of the viruses. Virus infection is detected by pattern recognition receptors like TLR7 that bind to single stranded RNA (ssRNA) viral replication intermediates in late endosomes. Here we report that TLR7 is expressed in BECs and detects RSV ssRNA, causing ERK MAP kinase signaling. RSV and influenza use this detection and signaling in BECs to drive its replication and infection, a mechanism that counters TLR7s role in antiviral defence. Experimental blockade of TLR7 binding or downstream signalling through ERK MAP kinase decreased RSV and influenza replication, but had no effect on HPIV3. RSV viral loads in mouse and human females were higher compared to males, consistent with higher sex-dependent expression of the TLR7 gene from two copies of the X chromosome in females. In a TLR7 gain of function mouse model there was a significant enhancement of RSV replication and RSV eosinophilic and Th2 disease markers like interleukin-5 (IL-5). In summary, TLR7 is expressed in human lung BECs in the lungs where it acts as a factor in RSV and influenza replication and disease pathogenesis. We propose that this is a major factor in determining the sex-disparity of viral disease.

papers.title: Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov. sp. nov., a new gut genus isolated from the stool of a healthy donor
papers.abstract: Strain Marseille-QA0792 (=CSUR QA0792, CECT 31199) was isolated from the feces of a healthy person using the culturomics method. The fecal sample originated from leftover material collected for a fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) procedure, obtained during a routine screening in accordance with the guidelines of the French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety (ANSM). This strain is Gram-stain-negative, rod-shaped, non-motile, and non-spore-forming. It is strictly anaerobic, with optimal growth at 37{degrees}C. Strain Marseille-QA0792 presented its highest 16S rRNA identity, 96.2%, with ''Merdibacter massiliensis'' strain Marseille-P3254 (not validly published) (accession number LT598590) and ANI similarity of 75.0% with the same species. Among validly published species, strain Marseille-QA0792 showed its highest 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity (91.5%) with Faecalicoccus acidiformans strain 37-2a (accession number HQ452864), whereas all computed average nucleotide identity (ANI) values were below 75%. Genome sequencing revealed a genome size of 2.67 Mb and a G+C content of 50.01%. This species is classified within the Erysipelotrichaceae family in the Bacillota phylum. Thus, we isolated for the first time a novel genus named Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov., sp. nov., strain Marseille-QA0792. This discovery highlights the importance of continuing culturomics efforts to explore the human microbiome.

papers.title: MoALE1, an ART-like effector, contributes to rice blast virulence through host immune suppression
papers.abstract: Rice blast, caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is one of the most destructive diseases affecting rice production worldwide. During infection, M. oryzae secretes effector proteins that suppress host immunity and facilitate colonization. Here, we characterized MoALE1, a predicted effector that is structurally similar to members of the heat-labile enterotoxin/cholera toxin family. Using a yeast secretion trap assay, we demonstrated that MoALE1 contains a functional signal peptide. A MoALE1-GFP fusion localized to the biotrophic interfacial complex, indicating that MoALE1 is a cytoplasmic effector. Expression analyses revealed that MoALE1 is expressed during biotrophy, from 16 to 48 h post-inoculation. Transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana showed that MoALE1 suppresses BAX-mediated cell death, suggesting a role in host immune suppression. To investigate its contribution to pathogenicity, a{Delta} moale1 mutant was generated and evaluated in rice infection assays. Deletion of MoALE1 significantly reduced disease severity but did not affect fungal growth, stress tolerance, sporulation, appressorium development, host penetration, or early invasive growth. In contrast, infection by the {Delta}moale1 mutant resulted in enhanced host H2O2 accumulation and increased expression of ROS-associated defense genes. Together, these findings identify MoALE1 as a biotrophy-associated cytoplasmic effector that promotes rice blast pathogenicity by suppressing host immune responses and provide new insight into the function of ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART)-like effector candidates in M. oryzae .

papers.title: Phosphate-responsive ornithine lipid biosynthesis remodels outer membrane composition and contributes to polymyxin tolerance
papers.abstract: Bacteria frequently encounter environments in which essential nutrients are limiting. Phosphate limitation constrains phospholipid synthesis and challenges maintenance of the cell envelope. While many Gram-negative bacteria respond by producing phosphorous-free membrane lipids, the mechanisms and consequences of this remodeling remain poorly understood in Enterobacterales. Here, we characterize the genetic and physiological basis of ornithine lipid (OL) biosynthesis in the opportunistic pathogens Enterobacter cloacae and Klebsiella pneumoniae. We show that OL biosynthesis depends on OlsF, a bifunctional acyltransferase that catalyzes both acylation steps required for OL synthesis. Phosphate limitation promotes OlsF-dependent OL accumulation through the PhoBR two-component system. Membrane fractionation revealed that OlsF-derived OLs are present in both membrane compartments but are enriched in the outer membrane. OlsF-dependent OL production enhances polymyxin tolerance during phosphate limitation, linking nutrient availability to changes in antimicrobial susceptibility. Together, these findings identify OlsF-dependent OL synthesis as a phosphate-responsive membrane remodeling pathway that reshapes outer membrane composition and influences the physiological properties of the Gram-negative cell envelope.

papers.title: Antibiotic-induced protein mislocalization drives hypervesiculation in Salmonella
papers.abstract: The incorporation of cytosolic proteins into bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) has remained mechanistically unresolved, as these proteins are normally excluded from vesiculation sites by the inner membrane (IM) barrier. Here, we show that antibiotic-induced envelope perturbation compromises this spatial barrier, enabling an aberrant interaction between proteins that are ordinarily segregated across cellular compartments and thereby promoting MV formation in Salmonella. Exposure to non-lethal cephalexin (LEX) induced robust hypervesiculation, accompanied by inhibition of the essential division penicillin binding protein (PBP) 3 and accumulation of the PBP5. Under envelope perturbing conditions, PBP5 accumulated at lateral sites associated with MV emergence and promoted periplasmic crowding independently of its catalytic activity. A cytosolic acyl carrier protein (ACP) emerged as a PBP5 interacting partner under LEX exposure, coinciding with cryogenic electron microscopy detected IM perturbation and aberrant ACP mislocalization. Formation of the PBP5 ACP complex promoted PBP5 accumulation, resulting in periplasmic crowding, progressive weakening of outer membrane peptidoglycan tethering, and ultimately MV formation. Together, these findings uncover a mechanism whereby stress-induced disruption of subcellular compartmentalization enables a non-canonical interaction between normally segregated proteins, driving hypervesiculation in Salmonella.

papers.title: High-throughput, single-cell-encoded colony imaging reveals infection-linked heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Phenotypic heterogeneity within bacterial populations shapes adaptation, antibiotic tolerance, and infection dynamics, yet colony-level quantification remains difficult at scale and on dark/selective media. We present HeteroTyper, an automated, high-throughput time-lapse platform that measures colony phenotypes across >100 plates per run on both transparent and dark media. HeteroTyper includes a ready-to-use computational pipeline that can be deployed on common plate-imaging setups and across agar types, delivering appearance times as a proxy for lag times, growth trajectories, colony size, intensity, and morphology from routine image series. Automated counts closely matched manual counts, supporting accuracy and scalability. Using Yersinia pseudotuberculosis as a model, HeteroTyper resolves phenotypic heterogeneity in vitro, with early and late phases showing broader appearance time distributions than mid-log phases. It also reveals organ-specific heterogeneity in vivo, with mesenteric lymph node isolates displaying the broadest appearance time distributions compared to spleen and liver. Appearance time was negatively associated with final colony size and intensity, linking growth initiation to downstream colony outcomes. Together, these distribution-level measurements indicate that bacterial adaptation during infection is compartmentalized by tissue microenvironments and prior history, and establish HeteroTyper as a practical, generalizable route to quantify infection-relevant phenotypic diversity on solid media at routine, high throughput.

papers.title: Rhizobia transform legume nodules via native T-DNA transfer systems
papers.abstract: Agrobacteria can deliver transfer DNA (T-DNA) into plant cells, causing tumorous growth. This process, agrobacteria-mediated transformation (AMT), underlies plant genetic engineering and has been regarded as an evolutionary innovation specific to these pathogens. By screening 63,759 alphaproteobacterial genomes for T-DNA border sequences, we identify mini-T-DNAs in diverse rhizobial genera. Each typically encodes a single cargo, a RolB/RolC family protein or a distant rhizobial homologue. We show that native rhizobia-mediated transformation (RMT) systems deliver these mini-T-DNAs into the root nodules of common bean, pea, and chickpea, where the cargo genes are expressed, with no signal in adjacent root tissue. RMT systems share VirG-dependent activation of the core virulence regulon but respond to distinct upstream signals. Our genome screen identifies many additional candidate T-DNA transfer systems, and phylogenetic analysis places their genes into two of the many type IV secretion system (T4SS) clades. RMT systems occur in both clades, together with other systems unrelated to T-DNA transfer, and typically have an ancestral-like T4SS configuration. In contrast, AMT systems occupy a single subclade, consistent with later acquisition of their T4SS module. AMT and RMT thus represent two specialized outcomes of an older, more widespread capability for bacteria-to-plant DNA transfer.

papers.title: A closed genome of Streptococcus agalactiae ST347/II reveals a composite integrative element coupling nisin P biosynthesis to erm(B) and tet(O) in Dominican group B Streptococcus
papers.abstract: Clindamycin is the alternative for intrapartum prophylaxis against group B Streptococcus in penicillin-allergic women, and whether it works depends on which lineages carry the resistance and on the mobile element that moves it. No Dominican group B Streptococcus genome has been closed. A Streptococcus agalactiae isolate from residual diagnostic material was sequenced twice on Oxford Nanopore, annotated, and screened against 83 genomes from a published Dominican maternal colonisation survey. The assembly is one circular chromosome of 2,066,859 bp with all seven rRNA operons resolved: ST347/CC19, serotype II, carrying erm(B), tet(O), mef(J) and msr(I). Two integrative conjugative elements were delimited: one of ~34 kb related to Tn5252 carrying erm(B) and tet(O), another of ~35 kb at a tRNA-Lys gene carrying mef(J) and msr(I). An eleven-gene class I lanthipeptide cluster lies 96 bp from the first element, on the same strand and with no annotated feature between them; its precursor encodes a 31-residue core identical to nisin P. The complete operon was found in 12 of the 83 genomes, 13 of 84 (15.5%) with the isolate. tet(O) was present in all 12 carriers and none of the 71 others (Fisher p = 1.03 x 10^-14), erm(B) in 12 of 12 against 3 of 71 (p = 4.70 x 10^-12). All eleven ST1 genomes lack both the operon and the nisin resistance protein; all 15 ST1010/IV genomes carry aac(6')-Ie/aph(2'')-Ia. Clindamycin resistance is therefore tightly associated with a lantibiotic-encoding element and contiguous with it in the one closed genome; in the drafts the relationship is statistical, and co-occurrence is not linkage. The ST1 absence predicts lineage-wide susceptibility, testable by deferred antagonism.

papers.title: Competence repression by the SPβ prophage in Bacillus subtilis revealed by transcriptomics across culture conditions
papers.abstract: Prophages are near-ubiquitous in bacterial genomes, yet their effects on host physiology are typically assayed under a narrow range of laboratory conditions, mostly involving DNA-damaging agents or physical and chemical stress. This leaves open the question of which ecological and physiological conditions trigger prophage-host interaction, and whether the outcome benefits the host or the prophage. Here, we used publicly available transcriptomic data to investigate conditions promoting prophage-host interaction in Bacillus subtilis. This analysis identified that competence strongly induces prophage gene expression. To further investigate the role of competence, we used two sets of B. subtilis strains: a natural SP{beta} lysogen strain and its cured counterpart, and a natural non-lysogenic strain and the same strain lysogenised with SP{beta}. Under competence-inducing conditions, both lysogen strains showed lower expression of the competence genes compared with their non-lysogenic counterparts. This result was corroborated by transformation assays that showed consistently lower transformation efficiency in the lysogen strains, and by fluorescence microscopy using a transcriptional reporter for the late competence gene. Because competence is a principal route for horizontal gene transfer in B. subtilis, prophage repression of the competence programme constrains host DNA uptake and evolvability. More broadly, these results show that mining public transcriptomes for condition effects can guide experimental effort towards prophage-host phenotypes that conventional laboratory conditions would miss.
